questions.question_text: Which is a valid boolean expression?
questions.explanation: 5 > 3 evaluates to the boolean true. Java booleans only hold true/false—you cannot assign an int (1) or a String to a boolean, and you cannot assign true to an int.

questions.question_text: What is the result of 9 / 4 * 4 in Java?
questions.explanation: Left to right: 9 / 4 = 2 (integer division), then 2 * 4 = 8. Integer division truncates the fraction first, so the result isn't 9—a classic order-of-operations trap.

questions.question_text: What does (int)(3.99) evaluate to?
questions.explanation: Casting a double to int truncates toward zero (drops the decimal), giving 3—it does NOT round. To round, you'd use Math.round(). Truncation vs rounding is heavily tested.

questions.question_text: What does "banana".indexOf("a") return?
questions.explanation: indexOf returns the index of the FIRST occurrence. In b(0)a(1)n(2)a(3)..., the first 'a' is at index 1. It returns the earliest match, not all matches.

questions.question_text: Which creates a new Scanner to read console input?
questions.explanation: A Scanner for keyboard input is constructed with System.in as the argument. The constructor needs a source; System.in is the standard input stream.

questions.question_text: What does "Hello".equals("hello") return?
questions.explanation: equals() is case-sensitive, so 'Hello' and 'hello' differ → false. Use equalsIgnoreCase() to compare ignoring case. equals returns a boolean, not a number.

questions.question_text: What prints? int n = 10; if (n > 5) System.out.print("big"); if (n > 8) System.out.print("huge");
questions.explanation: Both independent if conditions are true (10 > 5 and 10 > 8), so both print: 'bighuge'. These are separate ifs, not if-else, so both can execute.

questions.question_text: What does !(x >= 5) simplify to?
questions.explanation: Negating >= flips it to <: !(x >= 5) is x < 5. Negating a comparison reverses the operator AND the boundary inclusion—a common De Morgan-style simplification.

questions.question_text: What is the final value of x? int x = 1; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) x *= 2;
questions.explanation: x doubles three times: 1→2→4→8. The loop runs for i = 0,1,2 (three iterations), each multiplying x by 2.

questions.question_text: How many asterisks does this print? for(int i=1;i<=3;i++) for(int j=1;j<=i;j++) System.out.print("*");
questions.explanation: Inner loop runs i times: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 asterisks. This triangular pattern is a classic nested-loop trace—the inner count depends on the outer index.

questions.question_text: A while loop checks its condition:
questions.explanation: A while loop tests its condition BEFORE each iteration, so the body may run zero times. A do-while checks AFTER, guaranteeing at least one execution.

questions.question_text: The keyword 'this' inside a method refers to:
questions.explanation: 'this' references the object on which the method was called, often to distinguish a field from a parameter of the same name (this.name = name). It's an instance reference.

questions.question_text: If a class has no explicitly written constructor, Java provides:
questions.explanation: Java supplies a default no-arg constructor only if you write NONE yourself. Once you write any constructor, the default disappears—so adding a parameterized constructor can break new ClassName().

questions.question_text: The toString() method is typically used to:
questions.option_b: return a String representation of an object
questions.explanation: toString() returns a String describing the object, called automatically when an object is printed or concatenated with a String. Overriding it gives meaningful output instead of a memory hash.

questions.question_text: What does int[] a = {3, 6, 9}; a[1] = a[2]; leave a[1] as?
questions.explanation: a[2] is 9, so a[1] becomes 9. Assignment copies the value at index 2 into index 1; the array becomes {3, 9, 9}.

questions.question_text: What does this leave in arr? int[] arr = {1,2,3,4}; for(int i=0;i<arr.length;i++) arr[i] *= 2;
questions.explanation: Each element is doubled in place: {2,4,6,8}. The loop visits every index and multiplies that element by 2, modifying the array.

questions.question_text: Accessing arr[arr.length] throws an exception because:
questions.option_b: the last valid index is arr.length - 1, so arr.length is out of bounds
questions.explanation: For length n, valid indices are 0 to n-1, so arr.length is one past the end—ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Off-by-one errors with length are the most common array bug.

questions.question_text: Why must you use ArrayList<Integer> rather than ArrayList<int>?
questions.option_b: ArrayLists store objects, so primitives must use wrapper classes like Integer
questions.explanation: Generic collections hold reference types (objects), not primitives. Integer wraps int; autoboxing converts between them automatically when adding/retrieving. You can't write ArrayList<int>.

questions.question_text: list.set(2, "x") differs from list.add(2, "x") in that set:
questions.option_a: inserts a new element shifting others
questions.option_b: replaces the element at index 2 without changing the list size
questions.explanation: set() overwrites the existing element at the index (size unchanged); add(index, value) inserts and shifts everything right (size grows). Confusing the two causes off-by-one and size bugs.

questions.question_text: What does this sum? int[][] m={{1,2},{3,4}}; int s=0; for(int[] row:m) for(int v:row) s+=v;
questions.explanation: Nested enhanced for visits every element: 1+2+3+4 = 10. The outer loop iterates over rows (int[]), the inner over each value—a clean way to total a 2D array.

questions.question_text: For int[][] m = new int[4][2], what does m.length give and what does m[0].length give?
questions.explanation: m.length = number of rows = 4; m[0].length = number of columns in a row = 2. The first dimension is rows, the second is columns—keep the order straight.

questions.question_text: An abstract method is one that:
questions.option_b: is declared without a body and must be implemented by subclasses
questions.explanation: Abstract methods declare a signature with no implementation; concrete subclasses must override them. A class with abstract methods must itself be abstract and cannot be instantiated directly.

questions.question_text: If Dog overrides toString(), then 'System.out.println(new Dog())' calls:
questions.option_b: Dog's overridden toString() via dynamic dispatch
questions.explanation: println calls toString() on the object, and polymorphism dispatches to Dog's override (the actual object's version). This is why overriding toString() customizes printed output.

questions.question_text: Every class in Java implicitly inherits from:
questions.explanation: Object is the root superclass of all Java classes, providing methods like toString(), equals(), and hashCode() that subclasses can override. This is why any object can be treated as an Object.

questions.question_text: int p(int n){ if(n==0) return 1; return 2*p(n-1);} What is p(3)?
questions.explanation: p(3) = 2·p(2) = 2·2·p(1) = 2·2·2·p(0) = 8·1 = 8. This computes 2^n; the base case p(0)=1 stops it and the multiplications unwind.

questions.question_text: The Fibonacci recursion fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) requires how many base cases?
questions.explanation: Because each call references the two preceding values, you need base cases for both n=0 and n=1 to terminate. A single base case would still recurse infinitely on the other small value.

questions.question_text: Recursion and iteration are alike in that both can:
questions.option_b: repeat a process until a stopping condition is met
questions.explanation: Both repeat work toward a stopping condition—any iterative solution can be written recursively and vice versa. Recursion uses the call stack; iteration uses a loop variable, trading clarity against memory.

questions.question_text: What is the value of 5 + 3 + "x" + 2 + 4 in Java?
questions.explanation: Left to right: 5+3=8 (numeric), then 8+"x"="8x" (now String), then "8x"+2="8x2", +4="8x24". Once a String appears, + concatenates the rest—operator behavior depends on operand types.
